prompt: Match each accountability to its job
explanation: One owner of priorities, one team building the increment, one guardian of the process — and the team manages itself.

prompt: The Scrum Master assigns tasks to developers.

distractor.0: The team is self-managing: members decide internally who does what. The Scrum Master guards the process, never the task list.

explanation: False. Self-managing teams allocate their own work; the Scrum Master removes barriers and protects the process.
Commit, steer, inspect the product with stakeholders, then improve the process. Review looks outward; retrospective looks inward.

prompt: Which event inspects the product with stakeholders?

distractor.0: Planning commits to the goal — inspection happens at the end.
distractor.1: Dailies steer the Developers' own plan.
distractor.3: The retrospective inspects the process, within the team only.

explanation: The review demos the increment to stakeholders and adapts the backlog; the retrospective follows and improves how the team works.

text: Actual progress = sum of ___ durations of tasks ___ by time t.
explanation: Actual progress adds estimated durations of finished tasks — earned value. Using actual durations instead is the classic exam trap.

prompt: Burn-up actual progress is computed from how long finished tasks actually took.

distractor.0: It uses their estimated durations — finishing a 20-day-estimate task in 30 days still earns 20.

explanation: False. Earned value = estimates of completed work, which is why planned and actual lines are comparable.

instructions: Read the SUMIF helper, then predict actual progress at day 30.
code:
Planned = SUM(B2:B20)          // 200
Rate    = Planned / Duration   // 200 / 100
Actual  = SUMIF(Finish, "<=" & T, B)
// tasks finished by day 30: estimates 20, 10, 15
explanation: SUMIF adds estimates only for finished tasks: 20 + 10 + 15 = 45. Planned at day 30 is 60 — so the project trails.
hints: SUMIF filters by the finish column first.
Add the three estimates, not the day.
